tier_reason: icedland/disas-bench README (results commit 689f3c8, 2021-06-11) lists diStorm at 92.17 MB/s decode and 58.85 MB/s decode+format against Capstone, Zydis, XED, bddisasm, udis86 and BeaEngine; the harness is public (bench.py, make-all.sh, bench/distorm/main.c and Makefile) with gcc 10.3.0, -flto -O3 driver flags in the Makefiles and an i5-6600K stated, so it is reproducible and third-party run (by the iced author).

corrections.workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB .text section of Firefox 86.0.1's 64-bit xul.dll, throughput in MB/s (computed as bytes/1024/1024 per second). The README does not state the loop count: bench.py's built-in default is 20 passes over the 36.4 MiB section of the older 63 MB input/xul.dll checked into the repo, and with a custom file and no loop-count argument it scales the count to keep the same total bytes (about 9 passes over a 77 MB section, derived from bench.py). The Firefox 86 xul.dll itself is not in the repo.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Kubuntu 21.04, gcc 10.3.0, Rust 1.52.1 (disas-bench README). make-all.sh builds the C libraries with gcc and LTO: Capstone and bddisasm as CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, XED via mfile.py --opt=3 --extra-flags=-flto, diStorm via its own make/linux Makefile (current version: -fPIC -O2 -std=c99) with -flto prepended, BeaEngine patched to -O3 -flto, udis86 without LTO (it got slower). The C bench drivers (bench/*/Makefile) are built with -flto -O3; the Zydis driver is a CMake Release build with CFLAGS=-flto. The Rust drivers (bench/iced-x86/Cargo.toml, bench/yaxpeax/Cargo.toml) use a release profile with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1 and no target-cpu setting. C libraries and yaxpeax-x86 are pinned git submodules (last updated March 2021); iced is pulled unpinned from its git master at build time.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are from the iced author's disas-bench fork (June 2021, i5-6600K) with the diStorm submodule of March 2021; diStorm's last commit is 2021-12-18 (v3.5.3), so it is abandoned and instruction-set coverage added since then by other decoders was not checked. The diStorm README itself gives no numbers, only 'ultra fast' and a 2014 thesis quote ('chose diStorm3, which had the best performance'). The benchmark loop count is not stated (see workload). Each driver runs once per configuration (no repetitions or variance); the C drivers time CPU time with clock(), the Rust drivers wall time with millisecond resolution. The decode+format driver discards distorm_format64's output, but its time is well above decode-only (58.85 vs 92.17 MB/s), so formatting work is being timed. Formatters differ in output syntax between libraries. The yaxpeax author's later fork (i7-12700K, GCC 11, rustc 1.67 nightly, bar chart without numbers) shows diStorm at roughly 138 MB/s decode and 86 MB/s decode+format, still ahead of Capstone, XED, Zydis and bddisasm but behind iced and yaxpeax (values read off the bars, approximate). The comparison is decode/disassembly throughput against other disassembler libraries, not assembly speed against GNU as, NASM or MASM (the category's spec baseline); objdump/libopcodes was not tested.

notes: Numbers match the disas-bench README rows exactly; tier A holds (public harness, compiler, flags in the per-library Makefiles, CPU). Corrected the workload (the README does not say 20 loops; bench.py would use about 9 passes over the 77 MB section unless a loop count was passed) and filled in the flags the record had not inspected. Shortcomings: abandoned since 2021-12, one-shot timings, off-spec baseline (disassemblers, not GNU as/NASM/MASM).

The C bench drivers (bench/*/Makefile) are built with -flto -O3; the Zydis driver is a CMake Release build with CFLAGS=-flto. The Rust drivers (bench/iced-x86/Cargo.toml, bench/yaxpeax/Cargo.toml) use a release profile with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1 and no target-cpu setting. corrections.caveats: First-party run: disas-bench is a fork of athre0z/disas-bench (MIT, Joel Höner 2017) hosted in iced's own organisation, and the June 2021 results were committed by the iced author; the iced driver's Cargo.toml was written by the yaxpeax author. iced is pulled unpinned from git master at build time, so the measured version is whatever master was in June 2021. The benchmark loop count is not stated (see workload). Each driver runs once per configuration (no repetitions or variance); the C drivers time CPU time with clock(), the Rust drivers wall time with millisecond resolution. The decode-only driver never reads the decoded Instruction (only the decoder position advances), so LTO could drop some operand stores. The decode+format driver uses iced's SpecializedFormatter from the fast_fmt feature with db/dw/dd/dq output disabled and the output-buffer check turned off, the cheapest formatter iced offers, while the C libraries use their general formatters; formatted text differs between libraries. Capstone and BeaEngine have no decode-only mode. The yaxpeax author's later fork (i7-12700K, GCC 11, rustc 1.67 nightly, bar chart only) shows iced at roughly 357 MB/s decode and 217 MB/s decode+format, with yaxpeax-x86 about level on decode (values read off the bars). iced has no C or C++ API (it ships Rust, .NET, Java, Python, JavaScript/WebAssembly and Lua bindings), so C++ users need their own FFI shim. The five newest commits (2026-07-14) are dependabot dependency bumps. Decode/disassembly throughput against other disassemblers, not assembly speed against GNU as, NASM or MASM (the category's spec baseline); objdump was not tested.

notes: All quoted numbers match the README table; tier A holds on the public harness with flags in the Cargo.toml and Makefiles. Shortcomings to record: first-party run in iced's own fork, cheapest specialized formatter versus general C formatters, no C/C++ API, one-shot timings, loop count unstated (record's '20 loops' corrected), off-spec baseline.
